summary: At 37.8 square miles but only about 11,000 residents, Rancho Mission Viejo is one of the least dense incorporated places in coastal Southern California — a master-planned community carved from what was, until very recently, one of the last working cattle ranches in Orange County, the roughly 23,000-acre Rancho Mission Viejo ranch that operated continuously since the Spanish colonial era. That legacy shapes the landscape: rolling inland hills studded with coastal sage scrub, broad swaths of permanently conserved open space managed under a habitat conservation plan, and trail systems that thread through canyons connecting village-style clusters of homes rather than a single continuous grid. The geography means sunset views over the Santa Ana Mountains' western ridgelines from many vantage points, and the Pacific coast at San Clemente sits roughly ten miles southwest. With a median household income around $181,000 and a median home value near $1.04 million, the price-to-income ratio lands at about 5.7 — tight but more tractable than much of coastal Orange County — though median rent above $3,300 signals that even renting demands serious income. This is decisively a bedroom community; there is no major employment corridor within the city limits, and most working residents commute via the 241 toll road or I-5 toward Irvine, Laguna Niguel, or beyond. Average highs hovering around 72°F year-round with 9.4 hours of daily sunshine deliver the mild, dry monotony that defines inland south Orange County. The essential tension: a place engineered from scratch to integrate nature preserves and walkable village nodes, set within a commute reality that still revolves around car travel on toll roads.
